lead: Virtual memory lets a process use more memory than physically present by swapping pages between RAM and disk. Demand paging brings a page only when the process accesses it, reducing start‑up load. Copy‑on‑write shares pages between processes until one writes, saving RAM and I/O. These mechanisms are essential for running large applications on smartphones, for handling many web requests on a server, and for supporting multiple virtual machines on a single host.

blocks.text: Virtual memory abstracts the physical memory as a large, continuous address space. The operating system divides this space into fixed‑size pages (usually 4 KB). Only a subset of pages resides in RAM; the rest stay on secondary storage. Demand paging means a page is loaded only when the CPU tries to read or write an address that is not currently in RAM.

items: Page size is a power of two, simplifying address translation.
The page table maps virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers or marks the page as not present.
A page‑fault interrupt signals the OS that the required page is missing.

blocks.where: EAT is effective access time; p is page‑fault rate (probability of a fault per memory reference); ma is memory access time (time to read a word from RAM); pf_time is the average time to service a page fault, including disk I/O and table updates.

blocks.text: Demand paging reduces the amount of RAM needed at program start, which is why mobile phones can run many apps simultaneously and why cloud servers can host many containers on the same hardware.

items: CPU generates a virtual address and sends it to the MMU.
MMU looks up the page‑table entry. The entry shows ‘not present’, so the MMU raises a page‑fault interrupt to the OS.
OS selects a free frame or evicts a victim page using a replacement algorithm.
OS issues a read request to the Disk for the needed page.
Disk returns the page data to the OS.
OS updates the page‑table entry with the new frame number and sets the present bit.
MMU resumes the interrupted instruction, now translating to a physical address.

blocks.text: The time spent in steps 3‑5 dominates the page‑fault service time. If the fault rate is high, the effective access time grows sharply, leading to thrashing.

blocks.where: EAT is effective access time; p is page‑fault rate; ma is memory access time; pf_time is the average page‑fault service time.
0.001 is the fault rate; 100 ns is the RAM access time; 8 ms = 8 000 000 ns is the average service time for a page fault.

blocks.text: Copy‑on‑write (COW) is used when a process creates a copy of its address space, for example during fork(). Both parent and child share the same physical pages marked read‑only. When either process attempts to write, the OS copies the page to a new frame, updates the page‑table, and then performs the write.

items: Reduces memory usage for processes that soon exec a new program.
Improves performance of fork() in Unix‑like systems.
Used by virtualization platforms to share identical guest OS pages.

blocks.text: COW is an optimization; it does not change the logical view of memory for the processes. The mechanism relies on the hardware support for page‑level protection bits.

examples.question: Memory access time = 100 ns, page‑fault service time = 8 ms, fault rate = 0.001. Compute the effective access time of the system.
steps: Convert all times to the same unit (nanoseconds).
Apply the formula EAT = (1 − p) × ma + p × (pf_time + ma).
Plug in p = 0.001, ma = 100 ns, pf_time = 8 000 000 ns:
Add the terms: 99.9 ns + 8 000.1 ns = 8 100 ns.
examples.answer: The effective access time is 8 100 ns (≈ 8.10 µs).
examples.check:
p = 0.001
ma = 100
pf = 8000100
EAT = (1 - p) * ma + p * pf
print(EAT)

traps: Treating the fault rate as a percentage of instructions instead of a probability per memory reference, which underestimates the impact of the long service time.
Adding the page‑fault time directly to the memory access time without weighting by the fault probability.
Confusing the page‑fault service time (disk I/O) with the time to update the page table; only the total service time belongs in the formula.
Assuming that a page fault always incurs a full disk read; in reality a dirty page may need to be written back first, increasing the service time.
Using megabytes (MB) instead of megabits (Mb) when quoting disk transfer rates, leading to a factor‑8 error.

quiz.q: What is the name of the hardware component that translates a virtual address to a physical address?
Explain why demand paging reduces the amount of RAM needed at program start.
quiz.a: Demand paging loads only the pages that are actually referenced. Unused pages remain on disk, so the initial RAM footprint is limited to the working set of the program.

quiz.q: A system has a page‑fault rate of 0.0005, RAM access time 120 ns and page‑fault service time 6 ms. Compute the effective access time.

A process experiences thrashing when its page‑fault rate exceeds 0.02. Which of the following actions can reduce thrashing? (i) Increase the number of frames allocated to the process, (ii) Use a larger page size, (iii) Run a different workload on the same machine.
quiz.a: (i) Increase the number of frames allocated to the process, and (iii) Run a different workload with a smaller working set. Larger page size (ii) is not a reliable method for reducing thrashing; it may help only in special cases, but generally it can worsen thrashing.

quiz.q: In copy‑on‑write, what protection attribute is set on the shared pages before a write occurs?
During a fork(), both parent and child share a 4 KB page marked read‑only. The child writes to the page. Describe the steps the OS takes.
quiz.a: 1) The write triggers a page‑fault because the page is read‑only. 2) The OS allocates a new free frame. 3) It copies the contents of the original page into the new frame. 4) It updates the child's page‑table entry to point to the new frame and marks it writable. 5) The write instruction is restarted.

beyond: Not for the exam. Virtual memory techniques are being extended to non‑volatile memory (NVM) where the line between RAM and disk blurs, enabling faster page‑fault handling. Research on adaptive page sizes and machine‑learning‑driven replacement policies aims to reduce thrashing on cloud workloads. Industry moves toward container‑aware memory managers that share pages across containers using COW, improving density in data‑center servers.
